lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the fate of free trade
lead.head: The shopkeeper’s last stand?

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 96

body: A week after mak­ing the case for free trade, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah turned to the ques­tion in the title: is glob­al­i­sa­tion doomed?
Shah began with a choice as old as na­tions. There is the mar­tial out­look, which grabs land, and the shopkeeper’s out­look, which trades its way to what­ever it wants.
“Every push in favor of au­tarky is tak­ing us closer to a mil­i­tary and a mar­tial out­look and a way to make progress by killing peo­ple,” he said. {096-C01}

The 1930s showed how. After the Smoot-Hawley tar­iffs and the re­tal­i­a­tion they pro­voked, world trade fell by 66 per cent. Varma said he could think of only one other thing that would do that: a world war.
## Built for a world of goods
After 1945 the GATT, a multi-country club, drove tar­iffs down. On man­u­fac­tures in de­vel­oped mar­kets they fell from 40 per cent in 1945 to under five, as Varma had noted the week be­fore.

It worked, Shah said, be­cause it left out farm­ing, be­cause trade then meant goods, be­cause big cor­po­ra­tions wanted open mar­kets, and be­cause the West had the lever­age to drag spoil­ers such as India along.

Every one of those pil­lars has since given way. Services now dom­i­nate the world’s economies, and trade rules barely reach them. “So re­ally it’s game over,” Shah said. “You move to ser­vices. Why han­ker after man­u­fac­tur­ing?” {096-C03}
Corporations lost in­ter­est, elites thought the bat­tle won, and after the Cold War the West cut the bud­gets that gave it lever­age.
## The China prob­lem

Then came China. Shah, a com­mit­ted free trader, laid out four wor­ries: sell­ing mil­i­tary ca­pa­bil­ity to a rival, choke­points such as drug in­gre­di­ents and rare earths, hid­den sub­si­dies that build mo­nop­o­lies, and a giant econ­omy ex­port­ing its debt trou­bles as cheap goods.
He set him­self a rule. “A per­son like me who is get­ting wor­ried about this must ex­plic­itly ar­tic­u­late sce­nar­ios of harm,” he said. {096-C05}
Varma dis­sented. If China sub­sidises cheap goods, he ar­gued, con­sumers save money that cre­ates jobs else­where, and the sub­sidy should be wel­comed.
## A shock to the sys­tem
Into this, Shah said, came “a sta­ble ge­nius called Donald Trump”, with tar­iffs on every coun­try at once and rates worked out from bi­lat­eral trade deficits, which he called non­sense.

The worse dam­age, Shah ar­gued, is un­cer­tainty. Wrecking sup­ply chains built over decades is “tan­ta­mount to throw­ing bombs on cer­tain present pro­duc­tion fa­cil­i­ties”, a cut in the world’s cap­i­tal stock. {096-C12}
The way for­ward, he said, is deep in­te­gra­tion: will­ing coun­tries, the rest of the OECD plus India, agree­ing rules so tight that cheat­ing is hard, with the door open to all who ac­cept them.
Nearer at hand, he sees a deep India-US free trade agree­ment as fea­si­ble, and he praised the Union government’s think­ing.
Varma went fur­ther. “My dream is that we have no tar­iffs at all,” he said. “Forget trade agree­ments, uni­lat­er­ally re­move all tar­iffs.” {096-C14}
Cars alone, he said, would be 30 per cent cheaper.
Shah ended on hope. “My dear friend Amit, I am op­ti­mistic that some­thing good is com­ing our way.”

second.label: Economic statecraft
second.head: Bitter pills from China
second.deck: Ajay Shah on India’s drug makers and a rival’s grip on their ingredients

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the Chinese API lever

body: India makes good-quality generic drugs for the world, but many of their raw in­gre­di­ents, called APIs, come from China. About 80 per cent of the world’s ca­pac­ity for mak­ing them sits there, Ajay Shah said. {#apis}

Ideally, an Indian firm such as Dr. Reddy’s buy­ing from a Chinese sup­plier would be a pri­vate deal. But Chinese firms are in­di­rectly con­trolled by the Communist Party, and Shah imag­ined a ne­go­ti­a­tion over Ladakh in which China threat­ens, in pri­vate, to cut off API ex­ports to India. {096-S04}

The daft re­sponse, he said, would be to hand one com­pany at a time a big con­tract. He, Vijay Kelkar and co-authors have worked out a de­sign that uses the state min­i­mally and with­out cor­rup­tion.

quote.text: When you have a vul­ner­a­bil­ity that turns into the power to threaten a gov­ern­ment.

third.head: Most favoured, least loved

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the most favoured nation

body: In the lan­guage of trade, “most favoured na­tion” is not a com­pli­ment. It is a piece of plumb­ing, Ajay Shah ex­plained, built into America’s 1934 trade law.
Some in Pakistan missed the point. Shah re­called amused com­men­tary in the Pakistani press about hawks out­raged that their coun­try treats India as its most favoured na­tion. {096-S02}

The rule says that if America cuts its tar­iff on pen­cils for Germany, it cuts it for ev­ery­body. That avoids a patch­work of rates, and goods sent through third coun­tries to ex­ploit it. {096-C02}

Amit Varma’s gloss: you treat ev­ery­one the way you treat your best friend. Since lower tar­iffs are bet­ter, he said, “this is a fab­u­lous way to in­cen­tivise”. Shah called it a kicker that builds a last­ing bias to­wards lower tar­iffs.

box.title: The column Ajay Shah answered
box.text: Robert Lighthizer’s *New York Times* col­umn of 6 February 2025 was, Ajay Shah said, the best thing he had read from the American right. Several peo­ple sent it to him ask­ing how he would re­spond, so he drafted a thor­ough re­but­tal. {#column}

sections.label: The aftermath
sections.head: Tariffs first, armies after
sections.caption: the road from Smoot-Hawley to war
body: In 1930 Herbert Hoover signed the Smoot-Hawley tar­iffs into law, though thou­sands of econ­o­mists and aca­demics had urged him not to. The United States raised tar­iffs on the rich coun­tries, they re­tal­i­ated, and world trade fell by 66 per cent.
Amit Varma called it a trade war with the ef­fect of a world war. Unemployment in America, he added, stayed at ten per cent through­out the decade. {#unemployment}

For Ajay Shah the road to war is di­rect. Shut out of trade, na­tions swap the shopkeeper’s out­look for the warrior’s: the Japanese in­va­sion of 1931, Italy’s con­quest of Ethiopia in 1935, the German idea of Lebensraum.
## The president’s pen

Hoover lost the elec­tion, and Roosevelt asked Congress for pres­i­den­tial au­thor­ity on trade, granted through the RTAA of 1934. That au­thor­ity, Shah said, is how Donald Trump comes to have so much power today. {096-S01}
The law rested on rec­i­proc­ity: America would cut tar­iffs when oth­ers cut theirs. That is not Ricardian the­ory, Shah said. Britain ruled the waves by cut­ting tar­iffs on its own.
But the law car­ried a kicker. Under most-favoured-nation treat­ment, a cut agreed with one coun­try ap­plied to all, cre­at­ing a steady bias to­wards lower tar­iffs ev­ery­where. {096-C02}
~ It had lit­tle time to work. Within a few years the world was at war again, and the re­think­ing began only from 1944.

quote.text: Roosevelt went to the Congress and asked for pres­i­den­tial au­thor­ity on trade, au­thor­ity that per­sists still today.

sections.label: The GATT years
sections.head: A club that ran out of steam
sections.caption: why the GATT worked, and stopped
body: From 1944, Ajay Shah said, John Maynard Keynes and Harry Dexter White began dream­ing up the post-war world. One piece was the GATT, a multi-country club to drive trade lib­er­al­i­sa­tion ev­ery­where.

It worked partly be­cause its de­sign­ers gave up on agri­cul­ture rather than fight farm lob­bies. Japan’s rice farm­ers, Shah said, are “a lethal lobby”, about two per cent of the pop­u­la­tion in a coun­try mak­ing semi­con­duc­tors. {096-J10}

In 1945, trade meant goods; there were no com­put­ers and no fibre-optic ca­bles. Global cor­po­ra­tions lob­bied for open mar­kets. And the West used mil­i­tary and aid lever­age to coax spoil­ers along, India among them.
## How it un­rav­elled

Each pil­lar has since cracked. In the me­dian coun­try, ser­vices are 67 per cent of GDP, and 71.5 per cent across the OECD, yet trade rules barely touch them. {#services} Shah would even give up a lit­tle man­u­fac­tur­ing for sweep­ing free trade in ser­vices.

Corporations, their goods agenda done, lost in­ter­est. Elites as­sumed the bat­tle was won. After the Cold War the West cut its mil­i­tary, for­eign-policy and aid bud­gets, and lost lever­age in a WTO where every coun­try holds a veto.
“One dinky coun­try can be a hold up,” Shah said.
~ For Amit Varma, the les­son of both episodes was that progress can­not be taken for granted.

quote.text: The West was pro­duc­ing that global pub­lic good all these years, and ba­si­cally the West ran out of en­ergy.

sections.label: The wrinkles
sections.head: A free trader’s four worries
sections.caption: China and the limits of free trade
body: Ajay Shah is a free trader with four wor­ries, and a rule for him­self: any­one who raises such wor­ries must spell out con­crete sce­nar­ios of harm. {096-C05}
The first is war: why sell an enemy the means to fight you? The sec­ond is the choke­point. India’s drug mak­ers de­pend on Chinese in­gre­di­ents, and China is “a party that has a coun­try”.

Third, hid­den sub­si­dies, from cheap credit to seized land, let Chinese firms dom­i­nate sim­ple prod­ucts like solar pan­els. Lost know-how is slow to re­build. “Economic de­vel­op­ment is not a man­ual, it’s learn­ing by doing,” Shah said. {096-C08}
Fourth, a giant econ­omy that an­swers its debt over­hang by flood­ing the world with cheap goods is ex­port­ing its un­em­ploy­ment.
## Varma’s dis­quiet
Amit Varma first steel­manned Shah’s case, stat­ing it so well that Shah could have made it him­self. {096-C17} Then he dis­sented, ask­ing how Adam Smith and David Ricardo would see it.

Cheap im­ports may shut local fac­to­ries, he said, but con­sumers save money, and that money cre­ates eco­nomic ac­tiv­ity and jobs. “If they are sub­si­diz­ing us, let us take the sub­si­dies with open arms.” {#openarms}

~ They clashed over mo­nop­o­lies. Varma said no firm has ever won a mo­nop­oly with low prices and then raised them with­out state co­er­cion. Shah replied that a $19-trillion one-party state is a new sit­u­a­tion. {#trillion}

quote.text: Like be­tween India and the UK, this would never hap­pen.

sections.label: The Trumpist case
sections.head: Not every rule is a wall
sections.caption: the Trumpist case against free trade
body: Most of what the American right writes on trade is poor, Ajay Shah said, but a col­umn by Robert Lighthizer was the best he had read. Shah read out its core: un­fair trade means sub­si­dies, mar­ket ac­cess lim­its, “rigged health and safety stan­dards”, di­rected bank­ing, cur­rency ma­nip­u­la­tion and lax en­vi­ron­men­tal rules.
Amit Varma gave Europe’s GDPR as a com­monly al­leged non-tariff bar­rier, re­call­ing J. D. Vance protest­ing it.
## Birthrights and bar­ri­ers

Shah sep­a­rated the strands. GDPR binds European and for­eign firms alike. On a visit to Sahyadri Farms in Nashik, the hosts learnt that grapes bound for Europe may get no pes­ti­cides for two months be­fore har­vest. {096-S06}
French grow­ers face the same rule, Shah said, and a democ­racy choos­ing a high safety stan­dard is ex­er­cis­ing its birthright.

Each coun­try also sets its own bal­ance on pol­lu­tion, labour and taxes, so India’s lower stan­dards are no sub­sidy. “You can’t take today’s Swedish stan­dard and apply that to India,” he said. {096-C10} Carbon diox­ide, a global pol­lu­tant, is the ex­cep­tion.

~ Real non-tariff bar­ri­ers exist, he said, such as India’s data-localisation rules, which keep out good for­eign cloud providers and raise costs for Indians. Some of Lighthizer’s case holds; some is “mumbo jumbo”.

quote.text: Now that’s a level play­ing field whether you grow grapes in France or you grow grapes in Nashik.

sections.label: The tariffs
sections.head: Eggs, deficits and bad maths
sections.caption: the Trump tariffs
body: The tar­iffs came on every coun­try at once, which needed a ne­go­ti­at­ing ca­pa­bil­ity that is un­likely to exist, Ajay Shah said. Then Donald Trump changed his mind: a 10 per cent tar­iff on ev­ery­body, and 145 or 245 per cent on China. {#tariff245}

Trump treats a bi­lat­eral trade deficit as a mea­sure of a country’s non-tariff bar­ri­ers. Shah re­called Amit Varma’s favourite il­lus­tra­tion: Varma runs a deficit with the shop that sells him eggs, which never buys the ser­vices of a prom­i­nent pod­caster. {096-J03}
The of­fi­cial who pub­lished the for­mula had an Indian name, Varma noted. “If you’re watch­ing this, learn some math, bro,” he said. “While you’re work­ing for Trump.” {096-J02}
## A gun to both heads

Chinese goods ex­ports to America are about $550 bil­lion, Shah said, some 2.8 per cent of China’s GDP. {#chinaexports} A trade war over them is “like two peo­ple hold­ing a gun at each other’s heads”.

Shah spot­ted the irony. He had wor­ried about the Chinese Communist Party cut­ting off goods to the world. “Well, here you’ve got the Republican Party block­ing the sale of those Chinese things into America.” {096-J06}
~ The deeper dam­age is un­cer­tainty: if the United States can do this, firms won­der, what might it do next? Every com­pany plan­ning its next fac­tory, Shah said, has a headache.

quote.text: There is no tar­iff on Russia, and there are tar­iffs on coun­tries that have no peo­ple.

sections.label: The way forward
sections.head: Wanted: a new Keynes
sections.caption: deep integration and India’s chance
body: The GATT was right for 1945, Ajay Shah said, but the world now needs deep in­te­gra­tion: will­ing coun­tries agree­ing rules on sub­si­dies, di­rected bank­ing, cur­rency ma­nip­u­la­tion, in­tel­lec­tual prop­erty theft and car­bon, so tight that cheat­ing is hard. {096-C13}

The Trans-Pacific Partnership was con­ceived this way, as a WTO 2.0 with an open ar­chi­tec­ture. Shah would leave out the Chinese Communist Party and a United States los­ing its ca­pa­bil­ity, and build the core from the rest of the OECD plus India.

Bangladesh, Sri Lanka or Pakistan could join later, on take-it-or-leave-it terms. When Shah said Keynes would be dream­ing of such a deal, Amit Varma replied: “In the long run, Keynes is right.” {096-J13}
## India’s mo­ment

Short of that, Shah sees a deep India-US free trade agree­ment as fea­si­ble. Donald Trump could claim he had fixed fif­teen ways in which India was not a good cit­i­zen of world trade; India could say it had se­cured a good deal.
India has al­ready of­fered an olive branch, he said, scrap­ping the 6 per cent equal­i­sa­tion levy, the Google tax, “which I al­ways thought was a dumb idea”. {096-S08}
~ After India and the US, Shah asked, why not the UK, the EU and Japan? Varma said an­other great open­ing “would please the soul of Manmohan Singh”.

quote.text: But now we are here. We’ve got many years of ex­pe­ri­ence, and now we need to think of deep in­te­gra­tion.
The priv­i­lege of in­ter­na­tional trade does not come from ex­port­ing. The priv­i­lege of in­ter­na­tional trade comes from the glory of being able to buy cheap things from over­seas.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Tanks, iPhones, old cars and a tearful flight: the episode’s tales

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s flight from Spain, and the show that broke him
stories.head: Tears in business class
body: Amit Varma flew to Spain re­cently, treat­ing him­self to busi­ness class on Etihad. He loves flights, he said, be­cause there is no in­ter­net and you can get use­ful work done. On the way back he watched *Adolescence* on his iPad.

Each of its four episodes is shot in one take. At first Varma thought it a gim­mick. Within a cou­ple of min­utes he de­cided it was es­sen­tial: be­cause there are no cuts, he said, “your at­ten­tion also never cuts”.

Varma re­called once rec­om­mend­ing Krzysztof Kieślowski’s *Dekalog*, ten films for Polish tele­vi­sion and “a web se­ries be­fore the web”, which he thought a pin­na­cle of cin­ema. Later *The Wire* brought a nov­el­is­tic ethic to the screen. *Adolescence*, he said, is a new pin­na­cle.

The first half of the fourth episode undid him. “In terms of sto­ry­telling craft, in terms of the way it was shot, in terms of the act­ing, I have never seen some­thing so good,” he said. He was weep­ing on the flight. {096-S10}

Nearby pas­sen­gers looked at him as if to ask how one of the luck­i­est peo­ple ever could be cry­ing. “You can have all the cham­pagne you want,” he said, “though of course I never drink.” {096-J11}

The show had mean­while be­come a po­lit­i­cal foot­ball. The right made an iden­tity-politics point about a white boy ac­cused of killing; oth­ers faulted it for cen­tring the ac­cused boy rather than the vic­tim.
~ Varma, cit­ing a line he at­trib­uted to Martin Amis, said the worst crit­i­cism faults an au­thor for not writ­ing the book you want. {096-J23} The show, he said, is about the human con­di­tion.
stories.why: Varma of­fered the show as proof of a golden age of cul­ture: a mas­ter­piece can be hugely pop­u­lar, and *Anora* won the Oscar. Engaging with it, he told Ajay Shah, is en­gag­ing with the hu­man­i­ties. {096-C18}
stories.postscript: Shah promised to watch only episode one. “Four hours is a huge com­mit­ment,” Varma con­ceded. {096-J12}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on weeping over Adolescence

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on 1980s India and the hidden price of tariffs
stories.head: Second-hand, first in price
body: In 1980s India, Amit Varma re­called, a sec­ond-hand car cost more than a new one, be­cause a new car took seven years to be de­liv­ered. {096-S09}
A tele­phone meant a seven-year wait too, and ev­ery­thing was ex­pen­sive, “even for elite like we were”. The open­ing up of 1991 changed that.

People nor­malise such costs, Varma ar­gued, and stop see­ing them. Today’s tar­iffs and non-tariff bar­ri­ers are just as hid­den. Remove them, he said, and cars would be 30 per cent cheaper: the car he bought for ten lakhs would have cost seven. {#cars}

~ Electronics would be cheaper too, and pretty much ev­ery­thing would be cheaper and bet­ter. He would do it uni­lat­er­ally. “All tar­iffs all coun­tries. That’s good for our peo­ple. Think only of our peo­ple,” he said.

quote.text: We had nor­mal­ized that world where a sec­ond­hand car would cost more than a new car.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the seven-year wait for a car

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on supply chains rewired overnight
stories.head: Packed to the gills in Madras
body: As the tar­iffs on China landed, Ajay Shah said, news­pa­pers re­ported that Apple was fill­ing planes “to the gills” with iPhones and fly­ing them from Madras to America. {096-S07}
Under the new tar­iffs, ship­ping them from China to America made no sense. “This is just all going crazy,” Shah said.

The air­lift is one pic­ture of a wider shock. Large com­pa­nies are look­ing at their pro­duc­tion ar­range­ments and ask­ing what to do, with Donald Trump hold­ing great power till November 2026, and maybe be­yond.

~ Supply chains tuned over decades, with a fac­tory in Madras, an­other in China, an­other in Argentina and dis­tri­bu­tion in America, are in dis­ar­ray. Amit Varma added that un­cer­tainty changes how firms in­vest, plan and ex­pand.
stories.why: When pol­icy turns on a whim, firms spend ef­fort rout­ing around it in­stead of pro­duc­ing. Shah likened wreck­ing the global ar­range­ment to bomb­ing fac­to­ries: it re­duces the world’s cap­i­tal stock. {096-C12}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Apple’s iPhone airlift

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where trade ends and war begins
stories.head: Tanks to Ukraine, tools to Russia
body: Germany was send­ing Leopard 2 tanks to Ukraine. At the same time, Ajay Shah said, the ques­tion arose whether it should go on sell­ing Russia the pre­ci­sion ma­chine tools used to make T-90 tanks on the other side. {096-S03}
“Why would you arm the peo­ple who are fight­ing wars with you?” he asked. Pure free trade be­came hard to de­fend, and gov­ern­ments turned to ex­port con­trols on mil­i­tary and dual-use goods.
Dual-use goods lead into messy ter­ri­tory, he warned, be­cause so much mod­ern high tech­nol­ogy over­laps be­tween the con­sumer world and the mil­i­tary world.
~ Amit Varma framed it as two par­a­digms, the pos­i­tive-sum world of trade and the neg­a­tive-sum world of war. It is not a bi­nary, he said: the two will al­ways co­ex­ist. {#paradigm}
stories.why: Once war is real, sell­ing to who­ever pays col­lides with not arm­ing your enemy. In the Second World War America was “the ar­se­nal of democ­racy”; that ca­pa­bil­ity, Shah said, now sits in China. {096-J17}

quiz.q: What did ‘most favoured nation’ mean in America’s 1934 trade law, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: A tar­iff cut ne­go­ti­ated with one coun­try is ex­tended to every coun­try.

quiz.q: Why did the GATT’s designers leave agriculture out of the post-war trade club?
quiz.a: To avoid fights with small but lethal farm lob­bies, like Japan’s rice farm­ers.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s imagined negotiation over Ladakh, what does China threaten to cut off?
quiz.a: API ex­ports to India, the raw in­gre­di­ents its generic drug mak­ers de­pend on.

quiz.a: He runs a deficit with his egg seller, who never buys his pod­cast­ing ser­vices.

quiz.a: The 6 per cent equal­i­sa­tion levy, the so-called Google tax.

quiz.q: Why, as Amit Varma remembers the 1980s, did a used car cost more than a new one?
quiz.a: Because a new car then took seven years to be de­liv­ered.

glossary.def: Economic self-sufficiency: a coun­try shut­ting it­self off from trade.
A trade rule: a tar­iff cut for one ap­plies to all.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 96. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Herbert Hoover (Underwood & Underwood, public domain); Robert Lighthizer (Office of the President-elect, CC BY 4.0); Franklin Delano Roosevelt (Leon Perskie, CC BY 2.0); John Maynard Keynes (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); David Ricardo (Thomas Phillips, public domain); Donald Trump (Daniel Torok, public domain); Krzysztof Kieślowski (Alberto Terrile, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Adolescence
shelf.why: A TV se­ries whose one-take for­mat lets the ac­tion un­fold or­gan­i­cally, which Amit calls a new pin­na­cle in film­mak­ing and a story about the human con­di­tion, not ei­ther side’s pol­i­tics.

shelf.title: Dekalog
shelf.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
shelf.why: Ten films made for Polish tele­vi­sion, ‘a web se­ries be­fore the web’, which Amit calls the pin­na­cle of cin­e­matic sto­ry­telling, above even Kieślowski’s Three Colours tril­ogy.

shelf.title: The Wire
shelf.why: A show that ig­nores the habits of tra­di­tional cin­ema (no hook, no back­ground score, fif­teen or six­teen major char­ac­ters, a story un­fold­ing slowly over sea­sons) and proved that TV can do what a novel does.

shelf.title: Anora
shelf.why: He says the last 20 to 25 min­utes are ‘so masterful’.

shelf.title: Perfect Days
shelf.why: Wenders’s film pairs the striv­ing of sim­ply being at your work with mo­ments of si­lence and soli­tude we rarely get; Amit calls it ‘a film that could only be made by an old man’.

shelf.title: Want Free Trade? May I Introduce You to the Tariff
shelf.creator: Robert Lighthizer
shelf.why: It was the best piece he found from the American right.

shelf.title: Andrew Doyle’s tweet on Kemi Badenoch’s grilling
shelf.creator: Andrew Doyle
shelf.why: Amit likes Doyle a lot and calls him a great free-speech thinker.

shelf.title: Envisioning an India-US free trade agreement
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It records a strik­ing con­sen­sus on the American side that a deep free trade agree­ment with India is one of the few po­lit­i­cally fea­si­ble things in the US.

shelf.title: India’s supply chain vulnerability with Chinese APIs
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah and others
shelf.why: Ajay and co-authors on the gen­uine na­tional-security worry about Chinese sup­ply chains, and how to ad­dress it nar­rowly, cleanly and with min­i­mal state in­ter­ven­tion, rather than by dis­tort­ing the whole econ­omy or hand­ing one com­pany at a time a big con­tract.

shelf.title: The case for trade barriers against Chinese imports
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The writ­ten case be­hind the hosts’ most un­com­fort­able dis­agree­ment: why a com­mit­ted free trader like Ajay wor­ries about a sys­tem­i­cally im­por­tant, rule-breaking re­vi­sion­ist power.

shelf.title: Where did the Bombay Club go wrong?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is back­ground on why some in­dus­tri­al­ists choose pro­tec­tion over com­pet­ing in a global mar­ket.

shelf.title: Trade liberalisation: Looking beyond the WTO
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It sup­ports the episode’s case that the way for­ward is deep in­te­gra­tion among will­ing coun­tries rather than an­other sim­ple mul­ti­lat­eral round.

shelf.title: Egregious Indian protectionism against trade in services
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It ap­plies the ser­vices-trade ar­gu­ment to India’s own bar­ri­ers.

shelf.title: India: An agricultural trade powerhouse
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case for India’s stake in agri­cul­tural trade: the global mar­ket is the big­gest sta­biliser of food prices, which India’s on-off im­port and ex­port bans un­der­mine.

shelf.title: Two divergent measures
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is fur­ther read­ing on the un­cer­tainty di­men­sion of the cur­rent mo­ment.

shelf.title: Implications of US tariffs
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: It is Ajay’s writ­ten take on what the tar­iffs mean, as a com­pan­ion to the episode’s dis­cus­sion.

shelf.title: The Globalisation Episode (Episode 95)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ foun­da­tional think­ing on glob­al­i­sa­tion: first prin­ci­ples, a pot­ted in­tel­lec­tual his­tory up to the Second World War, and why tar­iffs harm a country’s own peo­ple and shift wealth from the poor to the rich.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s mas­ter­class on the power sec­tor: solar, wind, stor­age and time-of-day pric­ing, why elec­tric­ity prices must be al­lowed to move, and why fix­ing Indian power is a 25-year jour­ney that Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing de­pends on.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: The Reformers (Episode 28)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The human story of the peo­ple who worked be­hind the scenes, often for decades and with­out re­ward, to open India up in 1991.

laughs.text: Amit on his bad hair day: ‘When I started The Seen and the Unseen... they would ask me why an audio pod­cast and I would say I have a face for audio. I have re­al­ized today... I also have a head for audio.’ He also de­scribes wash­ing his hair and then work­ing to make it look ‘nat­u­rally uncombed’.

Amit on the tar­iff for­mula: one of the of­fi­cials who pub­lished the math had an Indian name, and some­one on Twitter joked, ‘just imag­ine they hired the one Indian who doesn’t know math.’ Amit adds: ‘If you’re watch­ing this, learn some math, bro. While you’re work­ing for Trump.’

Ajay, re­call­ing Amit’s favourite il­lus­tra­tion of why bi­lat­eral deficits are mean­ing­less: ‘I have a bi­lat­eral trade deficit with my local shop that sells me eggs be­cause I only buy eggs from him and he never buys the ser­vices of a prom­i­nent pod­caster.’
Ajay on the tar­iff roll­out: ‘Into this came a sta­ble ge­nius called Donald Trump.’ After Trump started ex­empt­ing phones and CPUs, he says: ‘this is ev­ery­thing but a sta­ble ge­nius.’
Ajay on the poor prepa­ra­tion be­hind the tar­iffs: ‘there is no tar­iff on Russia, and there are tar­iffs on coun­tries that have no peo­ple.’

Ajay points out the irony: he had wor­ried about the Chinese Communist Party cut­ting off goods to the world, ‘Well, here you’ve got the Republican Party block­ing the sale of those Chinese things into America.’
Ajay on Japan’s farm lobby: rice farm­ers are ‘a lethal lobby’, about two per­cent of the pop­u­la­tion, in ‘the coun­try that is mak­ing semi­con­duc­tors. But why pick fights?’

Amit says Ajay agreed to watch an episode of Adolescence on his iPad after the shoot ‘and then found a way to wrig­gle out’, and de­mands ‘a pub­lic com­mit­ment, Ajay Shah, that be­fore the air­ing of this episode you will watch Adolescence.’ Ajay com­mits only to episode one, and Amit con­cedes that four hours ‘is a huge com­mit­ment.’

When Ajay says Keynes would be dream­ing of a deep, open trade agree­ment, Amit quips, ‘In the long run, Keynes is right,’ a twist on Keynes’s own ‘in the long run’ line. Ajay sighs: ‘Sadly, we don’t have a John Maynard Keynes today.’

‘Make love, not war’: Ajay bor­rows the slo­gan for the shopkeeper’s out­look. He con­trasts it with Britain, the ‘na­tion of shopkeepers’ that built navies and a trad­ing sys­tem, and says ‘Britannia ruled the waves’ be­cause it uni­lat­er­ally cut tar­iffs.
‘The ar­se­nal of democracy’: the World War II phrase for America’s man­u­fac­tur­ing might, which Ajay says now sits in China.
Joan Robinson’s metaphor, in­voked by Amit for uni­lat­eral free trade: ‘we’ve put rocks on our own coast­line, re­move the rocks.’

Martin Amis, as re­called by Amit: ‘the worst kind of crit­i­cism is when you crit­i­cize an au­thor for not writ­ing the book you want.’ Amit uses it against crit­ics who fault Adolescence for cen­tring the ac­cused boy rather than the vic­tim.
